To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Support Vector Machine (SVM) is the most accurate algorithm for classification of SSH attacks with a 95.2% accuracy.
the machine learning algorithm J48 decision tree outperforms all other algorithms in the case of SSH attack classification.

the Naive Bayes Learner algorithm is the most effective in classifying the "not-so-sever" attacks, whereas the Support Vector Machine algorithm is the best for classifying the "severe" category of attacks.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the classification of attacks from a compromised server and the performance evaluation of machine learning algorithms.
the classification of SSH attacks using machine learning algorithms and the performance evaluation of the same using the selected features.
the classification of SSH attacks into two classes: "severe" and "not-so-sever" attacks.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the performance of the machine learning algorithm is not affected by the presence or absence of the attack activities from a compromised server.
the machine learning algorithms can be used to segregate the SSH attack types with a reasonable level of confidence.
the performance of the Naive Bayes classifier outperforms all other algorithms in the classification of SSH attacks.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
Naive Bayes classifier outperforms other algorithms for the given dataset.
, the Naive Bayes classifier performs well in classifying severe attacks with 98.8% accuracy, 98% sensitivity, 100% precision, and 99% F-score.
the machine learning algorithms can classify SSH attacks with a high degree of accuracy.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, we could segregate SSH attacks into two categories, severe and not-so-severe using the network flows, which is not possible with the existing work.
, the attacks from a successful compromise of SSH server are different from other attacks in the network flows and hence they could be segregated.
we have been able to segregate the "severe" SSH attacks from other attacks using network flow data.
